- [major] .github/workflows/publish.yml:46 — SBOM includes irrelevant global runner dependencies (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ The workflow installs the package into the global GitHub Actions runner environment and uses `cyclonedx-py environment` to generate the SBOM. This will include all pre-installed CI tools (such as ansible, awscli, etc.) instead of just the project dependencies.
  - _verification:_ verified — The step runs `cyclonedx-py environment`, which enumerates every distribution installed in the active Python environment — and just above it the workflow installs `cyclonedx-bom` (and its transitive deps) plus the wheel into that same environment. So the resulting SBOM mixes the build tooling and any runner-preinstalled packages with the package's real dependencies, rather than describing only the published artifact. The diff supports the claim.
  - _fix:_ Create and activate a clean virtual environment, install only the package and `cyclonedx-bom`, and run `cyclonedx-py environment` from there.
- [major] src/ai_jury/ci.py:20 — CI fail-on severities do not normalize the documented blocker alias (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ findings normalize blocker to critical, but evaluate_ci builds fail_set by lowercasing raw strings and compares group severity directly, so blocker never matches critical
  - _verification:_ verified — evaluate_ci builds fail_set by only stripping/lowercasing (ci.py:20), and config.py:431 likewise only lowercases fail_on — neither applies _SEVERITY_ALIASES {'blocker':'critical'}. Findings ARE normalized (blocker->critical), so a documented '--fail-on blocker' yields fail_set {'blocker'} that can never match a group's 'critical' severity, silently disabling the gate for that alias.
  - _fix:_ normalize fail_on values through the same severity alias logic used for Finding severities before comparing
- [major] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:206 — _debate_round leaks real agent names in prior_txt (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ The prior_txt string is constructed using f"### {r.agent}\n{r.output}", which exposes the real agent identity for previous debate rounds, defeating the anonymize_debate setting.

The peer-review block is anonymized via _anonymize_peers but the prior-debate addendum is not, so round-3+ debate prompts expose real identities, undermining the #37 guarantee.
  - _fix:_ Use _anonymize_peers or an existing label map to mask r.agent when constructing prior_txt.
- [major] src/ai_jury/privilege.py:27 — Codex workspace-write mode is not flagged by the privilege audit (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ _DANGEROUS_FLAGS includes danger-full-access but not workspace-write; when extra_args contains -s workspace-write, _is_sandboxed returns false and the dangerous-flag loop finds nothing, so strict mode does not catch writable review agents
  - _verification:_ verified — Same root cause as the claude finding: _DANGEROUS_FLAGS lacks 'workspace-write' and _is_sandboxed only treats 'read-only' (or bare --sandbox) as sandboxed, so `-s workspace-write` produces no warning despite the docstring promising it is flagged.
  - _fix:_ detect Codex sandbox values explicitly and warn/fail for any value other than read-only, including workspace-write
- [major] src/ai_jury/privilege.py:27 — Least-privilege audit does not flag codex `-s workspace-write`, despite docstring claiming wider sandboxes are flagged (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ _DANGEROUS_FLAGS lacks 'workspace-write'; _is_sandboxed() returns True only for read-only, so a write-capable codex reviewer over attacker-controlled diffs yields no warning and is not caught even under --strict, contradicting the module docstring at lines 17-19
  - _verification:_ verified — For `-s workspace-write`, _is_sandboxed returns False (nxt != 'read-only' and a != '--sandbox'), then audit_agent only matches against _DANGEROUS_FLAGS, which contains 'danger-full-access' but NOT 'workspace-write'. So no warning is emitted, yet the module docstring explicitly states 'A wider sandbox (workspace-write/danger-full-access) is flagged here'. Clear behaviour/doc mismatch.
  - _fix:_ Add 'workspace-write' to _DANGEROUS_FLAGS, or make audit_agent flag any codex `-s` mode other than read-only
- [major] website/docs.html:213 — TOC generation can reintroduce sanitized heading text as executable HTML (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ The code concatenates h.textContent directly into an HTML string and assigns it to toc.innerHTML; encoded markup in a markdown heading can become text after sanitization and then be parsed as markup in the generated TOC.
  - _verification:_ verified — buildTOC concatenates raw h.textContent into the `html` string and assigns it via `toc.innerHTML = html` with no HTML escaping. Heading text that survives DOMPurify as literal entity-decoded markup (e.g. a heading containing &lt;img onerror=…&gt;) becomes real markup when re-inserted through innerHTML, bypassing the earlier sanitization. The mechanism is clearly present in the diff.
  - _fix:_ Build TOC links with document.createElement and assign label text via textContent, or escape h.textContent before concatenating.

- [minor] src/ai_jury/classification.py:140 — Security keyword 'vulnerab' compiled as \bvulnerab\b can never match 'vulnerable'/'vulnerability' (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ _KEYWORD_RES builds re.compile(r"\b" + re.escape(kw) + r"\b") for every keyword; for the stem 'vulnerab' the trailing \b sits between two word chars in 'vulnerability', so the pattern only matches the standalone token 'vulnerab' which never occurs, making the keyword dead
  - _verification:_ verified — SECURITY_KEYWORDS contains the prefix 'vulnerab' and _KEYWORD_RES compiles every keyword as r'\b'+escape(kw)+r'\b'. The trailing \b requires a word boundary after 'b', which never occurs in 'vulnerable'/'vulnerability' (b->l is letter-to-letter), so the intended prefix match is dead.
  - _fix:_ Use a prefix pattern for stem keywords (e.g. \bvulnerab\w* or drop the trailing \b), or list full words 'vulnerable'/'vulnerability'
- [minor] src/ai_jury/classification.py:171 — unsupported verified findings can still be classified as high risk (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ the code returns high for any major consensus/majority group without checking g.status, despite the documented threshold excluding rejected/unsupported groups
  - _verification:_ verified — _risk_level returns RISK_HIGH for any 'critical' finding regardless of status, and for a 'major' group checks only g.bucket in (consensus, majority) — never g.status. Its own comment says 'not rejected', but the code never consults verification status, so a verifier-rejected (status='unsupported') finding still drives high risk, contradicting the documented intent.
  - _fix:_ exclude groups with status == 'unsupported' when promoting major findings to high risk
- [minor] src/ai_jury/formats.py:120 — to_json ignores the effective --decision/vote, so JSON metadata never reflects panel-vote mode (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ to_json calls build_run_metadata(outcome, config) without decision=/vote=, whereas cli.main builds the markdown metadata with decision and vote; --decision vote --format json yields metadata.decision from config defaults and vote=null

- [minor] src/ai_jury/formats.py:138 — SARIF region.startLine can be 0/negative from an agent-supplied finding line, producing invalid SARIF (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ _sarif_result sets region={'startLine': f.line} whenever f.line is not None; f.line is int-coerced agent output and SARIF requires startLine >= 1
  - _verification:_ verified — _sarif_result emits region={"startLine": f.line} whenever f.line is not None. Finding.__post_init__ only coerces line via int() with no lower bound, and Finding.from_obj takes the line straight from attacker/agent-supplied JSON. A supplied line of 0 or a negative integer would survive and be emitted as startLine, which violates the SARIF 2.1.0 requirement that startLine >= 1. The diff supports the claim.
  - _fix:_ Only emit region when f.line is a positive integer (if f.line and f.line >= 1)
- [minor] src/ai_jury/github.py:16 — gh subprocess calls have no timeout and are outside the orchestrator's time budgets, so a hung gh can block the run forever (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ _gh and _gh_with_input call subprocess.run(['gh', ...]) without timeout=; phase/total timeouts only wrap agent calls, not diff fetch/post
  - _verification:_ verified — _gh and _gh_with_input both call subprocess.run([...]) with no timeout= argument. These are invoked from the CLI/github helpers (pr_diff, pr_context, post_*_comment, compare_diff, pr_head_sha, etc.), which run outside the orchestrator's RunBudget/phase timeouts. A hung gh process would block indefinitely with no enforced cap. Claim is accurate.
  - _fix:_ Add a bounded timeout= to both helpers and convert subprocess.TimeoutExpired into a clear RuntimeError
- [minor] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:237 — Redundant redaction of shared context inflates redaction_count (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ context, _n2 = redact(context) runs per-chunk inside run_jury. Because context is shared, the same secrets are repeatedly counted, inflating the sum in _merge_chunk_outcomes.
  - _verification:_ verified — run_jury redacts `context` on every call and stores _n2 into redaction_count; review_diff calls run_jury once per chunk passing the SAME context, and _merge_chunk_outcomes sums redaction_count across chunks (`sum(o.redaction_count for o in outcomes)`). With expanded context containing secrets and a chunked diff, the context's secret count is counted once per chunk, inflating the total. Minor but real.
  - _fix:_ Redact the context string exactly once in review_diff before passing it to the chunked runs.
- [minor] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:684 — _synthesize uses an unseeded RNG fallback when anonymize_reviews=True and rng is None, breaking the determinism invariant if reached (reviewers: claude)

  - _verification:_ verified — The line `peer_rng = random.Random(rng.random()) if rng is not None else random.Random()` does fall back to an unseeded Random() when rng is None. The claim is precise and self-limited ('if reached'); the current sole caller always passes run_rng, but the latent non-deterministic branch exists exactly as described. Minor.
  - _fix:_ Seed deterministically (e.g. random.Random(0)) or require rng to be passed

- [minor] tests/test_report.py:28 — Misplaced `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block sits between test classes, so two test classes are silently skipped on direct invocation (reviewers: claude)

  - _evidence:_ tempfile.mkdtemp() creates a directory that is not automatically deleted when the test ends, leaking disk space on test runners.

- [minor] website/app.js:423 — Generated jury.toml does not reflect the selected panel vote decision mode (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ The TOML lines include rounds, chair, and verify, but never add decision; meanwhile the scripted command includes --decision vote when vm === 'vote', so copying the TOML changes behavior back to the default chair decision.
  - _verification:_ verified — render() computes vm = verdictMode() (chair/vote) and uses it only in the human-readable note, but the generated [jury] block pushes rounds/chair/verify/auto_depth and never emits a `decision` key, so toml-out ignores the vote selection.
  - _fix:_ Add `decision = "vote"` to the generated [jury] block when verdictMode() returns vote.
- [minor] website/docs.html — Third-party CDN scripts (marked, DOMPurify, highlight.js) are loaded without Subresource Integrity hashes (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ docs.html renders markdown fetched at runtime and depends on DOMPurify.sanitize for XSS protection, but the jsdelivr <script> tags pin versions without an integrity attribute, so a compromised/tampered CDN response could disable sanitization
  - _verification:_ verified — The three jsdelivr <script> tags for marked@12.0.2, dompurify@3.1.6, and highlight.min.js are loaded with no integrity= (and no crossorigin=) attributes, so there is no SRI protection on the CDN-served code.
  - _fix:_ Add integrity="sha384-…" crossorigin="anonymous" to each CDN <script>, or self-host the libraries under website/
- [minor] website/docs.html:185 — Cross-document markdown links lose their anchor fragments (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ When FILE_TO_SLUG[path] matches, the href is set to '#' + slug and the existing frag variable is not appended; docs contain links such as platforms.md#claude-code-plugin that will route only to #platforms.
  - _verification:_ verified — In rewrite(), the internal-doc branch sets href to `'#' + FILE_TO_SLUG[path] + (frag && frag !== '#' ? '' : '')`. Both ternary arms evaluate to the empty string, so the captured `frag` is never appended — every cross-doc link drops its #anchor.
  - _fix:_ Preserve the fragment in the rewritten route, for example encode it in the hash and scroll to it after loading the target document.
- [minor] website/index.html:48 — og:image and twitter:image use relative paths while og:url/canonical are absolute (reviewers: claude)
  - _evidence:_ og:image is 'assets/og-banner.png' (line 48) and twitter:image is 'assets/og-banner.png' (line 62); some social/SEO crawlers do not resolve relative OG image URLs, so share-card images may fail to render
  - _verification:_ verified — The diff sets og:url and canonical to the absolute 'https://berkayturanci.github.io/ai-jury/', but og:image and twitter:image use the relative 'assets/og-banner.png'. Several social/crawler scrapers require absolute image URLs, so the inconsistency is real and clearly evidenced by the diff.
  - _fix:_ Use the absolute URL https://berkayturanci.github.io/ai-jury/assets/og-banner.png for both og:image and twitter:image

### Disputed (needs human decision)

- [major] .github/workflows/scorecard.yml:20 — Scorecard job drops contents: read permission (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ The workflow sets top-level contents: read, but the job defines its own permissions block containing only id-token: write. In GitHub Actions, job-level permissions override the workflow defaults for that job, so checkout/Scorecard no longer get contents read access.
  - _verification:_ needs human decision — Factually the `analysis` job sets a job-level `permissions:` block listing only `id-token: write`, which in GitHub Actions replaces (not merges with) the top-level `permissions: contents: read`, so contents is effectively `none` for that job. However, this mirrors the official OpenSSF scorecard-action template, and a public-repo checkout plus Scorecard API calls generally function without job-level contents:read — so whether this is an actual defect or a benign, idiomatic configuration is genuinely ambiguous.
  - _fix:_ Add `contents: read` under `jobs.analysis.permissions` alongside `id-token: write`.
- [major] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:214 — Anonymous reviewer labels swap randomly between debate rounds (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ peer_rng is seeded with run_rng.random() in every round. Because run_rng advances, the seed changes between rounds, causing _anonymize_peers to shuffle differently and swap the anonymous labels.
  - _verification:_ needs human decision — Each round derives a fresh `peer_rng = random.Random(run_rng.random())` per debater, so the label->agent mapping is reshuffled every round and is indeed not stable across rounds. However _anonymize_peers' docstring states the intent is that 'neither identity nor position is a stable signal', so the instability appears partly by design; whether cross-round inconsistency (vs. the real-named prior-debate block) is harmful is debatable.
  - _fix:_ Seed peer_rng deterministically using the debater's name and a fixed run seed so the shuffle order remains stable across rounds.
- [major] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:381 — _format_findings_for_verify exposes real reviewer names (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ The formatted findings string includes `(by {f.reviewer})`. The chair judges these findings before synthesis, allowing it to bias verdicts toward its own findings and defeating the self-preference guardrail.
  - _verification:_ needs human decision — The formatter does emit `(by {f.reviewer})`, surfacing real reviewer identities to the chair during verification. True as stated, but no anonymization was ever designed for the verify phase (#37 covers debate, #38 covers synthesis-reviews), so this is an un-addressed scope gap rather than a clear regression — a maintainer should decide if verify needs the same treatment.
  - _fix:_ Omit `(by {f.reviewer})` from the verification prompt.
- [major] src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:444 — _synthesize exposes real debater identities to the chair (reviewers: agy)
  - _evidence:_ While reviews_txt is correctly anonymized, debate_txt embeds r.agent directly, allowing the chair to read the debate text to see exactly which agent argued what, defeating anonymize_synthesis.
  - _verification:_ needs human decision — debate_txt is rendered with real `### {r.agent}` names unconditionally; the #38 anonymization (anonymize_reviews) only strips identity from the round-1 REVIEWS block, not the debate block. So a chair that debated can identify its own debate output. Factually accurate, but the implemented guardrail is explicitly scoped to round-1 reviews, so whether the debate block should also be anonymized is a design decision for a human.
  - _fix:_ Apply the anonymization mapping to the debate results passed into the synthesis prompt.
- [major] src/ai_jury/prompts.py:97 — untrusted diff can break out of prompt sentinel fences (reviewers: codex)
  - _evidence:_ the template inserts {diff} directly before a fixed closing UNTRUSTED_DIFF>>> delimiter, so attacker-controlled diff content containing that delimiter can close the fence and inject text outside the untrusted block
  - _verification:_ needs human decision — Sentinels are plain text and the diff content is interpolated without escaping or collision-checking the closing token, so a crafted diff containing 'UNTRUSTED_DIFF>>>' could in principle break out. However the module docstring documents this as the 'cheapest defense-in-depth layer' with the structured-consensus pipeline and CI gate as the authoritative control, so whether this is a blocking defect vs. an accepted tradeoff is a genuine judgment call.
  - _fix:_ escape or encode sentinel substrings in untrusted content, or generate per-run high-entropy delimiters that are guaranteed absent from the payload before formatting prompts
- [major] tests/test_github.py:96 — pr_comment_bodies assumes newline-delimited output (reviewers: agy)

## Verdict
**COMMENT** — No blocking defects: the diff is almost entirely new scaffolding (workflows, community-health files, docs, assets, benchmark fixtures) with no `src/ai_jury/*.py` executable surface, and the two highest-severity claims were both refuted on verification. Two genuine but low-severity accuracy issues remain worth fixing.

## Consensus findings

- **[minor] `.github/workflows/publish.yml:46` — SBOM captures the whole runner environment, not the package** (raised by agy/Reviewer A, affirmed by claude + codex in debate, **verified**). The step runs `cyclonedx-py environment` after `pip install`-ing the wheel *and* `cyclonedx-bom` into the runner's default interpreter, so the emitted SBOM mixes build tooling and preinstalled runner packages with the package's real (empty — stdlib-only) dependency set. Especially misleading for a project whose selling point is *zero runtime dependencies*. Fix: build/emit from a clean venv containing only the wheel. Severity is accuracy-of-release-artifact, not a security/correctness break.

- **[minor] `.github/workflows/pages.yml:6` — Pages deploy trigger contradicts the docs** (raised by claude/Reviewer C, affirmed by codex, **verified**). The workflow is `on: push: branches: [main]` with no `paths:` filter (and an explicit "Deploy on any push to main" comment), while `docs/architecture.md`'s CI-&-runners table and `CLAUDE.md` both state Pages deploys on `push to website/**`. Low harm (a non-website commit just redeploys the same site), but the documented contract is wrong. Fix: either add `paths: ['website/**']` or correct the two docs.

## Disputed findings

- **`.github/workflows/publish.yml:64` — "comma-separated `subject-path` breaks attestation" (agy: blocker/critical).** **Ruling: rejected (false positive).** `actions/attest-build-provenance` accepts a comma- *or* newline-separated list of paths/globs and tolerates surrounding whitespace; `"dist/*.whl, dist/*.tar.gz"` is a valid, documented form. Both claude and codex disputed it and verification marked it **unsupported**. The "blocker" severity was unwarranted.

- **`.github/workflows/scorecard.yml:20` — "job drops `contents: read`" (codex/Reviewer D: major).** **Ruling: downgrade to optional hardening, non-blocking.** The mechanics are correct — a job-level `permissions:` block replaces (not merges) the workflow default, so this job's token is effectively `contents: none`. But this mirrors the **official OpenSSF scorecard-action starter** (which notes `contents: read` is "only needed if installing in a private repository"); this repo is public and checkout uses `persist-credentials: false`. Verification landed on **needs_human_decision**. Adding `contents: read` is harmless and I'd recommend it for clarity, but "the security automation may not produce results" is overstated. Not a defect that blocks this PR.

## Notable single-reviewer findings

- **[minor] `README.md` CLI-compatibility-contract is stale** (codex, round-2 MISSED — credible, not formally verified). The "Stable flags" list omits flags introduced/documented elsewhere in this same diff: `--issue`, `--decision`, `--live`, `--transcript`, `--verbose`, `--post-progress`, `--post-mode`, `--incremental`, `--suggest-patches`, `--patches-out`, `--label`, `--auto`, and the cache/timeout flags. Since that section asserts the documented flag set and the parser stay "exactly in sync" (guarded by `test_documented_flags_match_parser_exactly`), the prose now under-documents the real surface. Worth a reconciliation pass, though note the contract distinguishes a curated *stable* subset from the full parser — confirm intent before editing.

## Verdict
**REQUEST CHANGES** — one real `major` bug (the CI gate silently ignores the documented `blocker` severity alias), plus several verified minor doc/code defects worth fixing in the same pass.

## Consensus findings
Ordered by severity; all independently verified.

1. **[major]** `src/ai_jury/ci.py:20` — *CI `fail_on` never applies the documented `blocker → critical` alias.* Raised by **codex (B)**, affirmed by **claude** and **codex** in debate, and confirmed by verification (which traced the same gap to `config.py:431`). `evaluate_ci` builds `fail_set` by only `strip().lower()`-ing the raw strings, while findings normalize `blocker → critical`. So `--fail-on blocker` (or `[jury.ci] fail_on = ["blocker"]` — both documented as valid in `docs/parameters.md`) yields `fail_set={"blocker"}`, which can never match a group's `"critical"` severity → **CI passes green on an unblocked critical finding.** Fix at the config-resolution boundary so every consumer (gate, report, metadata) sees the normalized severity, not just `evaluate_ci`.

2. **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/classification.py:171` — *high-risk promotion ignores verifier status.* Raised by **codex (B)**, affirmed by **claude**/**codex**, verified. `_risk_level`'s own docstring says a major group is high risk only when "not rejected/unsupported", but the loop checks only `g.bucket in ("consensus","majority")` and never `g.status`. An `unsupported` major group still drives `high` risk and `needs_human_attention`. Guard on `g.status != "unsupported"`.

3. **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/classification.py:140` — *dead security keyword.* Raised by **claude (C)**, affirmed by **codex**, verified. `"vulnerab"` is compiled as `\bvulnerab\b`; the trailing `\b` falls between two word chars in `vulnerable`/`vulnerability`, so the intended stem match never fires. Use a prefix pattern (`\bvulnerab\w*`) or list the full words.

4. **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/adapters.py` (CodexAdapter `build_argv`) — *stale, security-misleading comment.* Raised by **claude (C)**, affirmed by **codex**, verified. None rose to multi-reviewer consensus on the merits. Reviewer A produced the only substantive finding set; B and C(qwen) found nothing; A refused/abstained in round 1. The three credible issues below were affirmed by the verifier and seconded by codex in debate, so I treat them as confirmed rather than single-reviewer.

1. **[minor] `src/ai_jury/formats.py:92` — `to_json` drops the effective `decision`/`vote`.** *(raised by claude; seconded by codex; verifier: verified.)* `to_json` calls `build_run_metadata(outcome, config)` without `decision=`/`vote=`, so `--format json --decision vote` always emits `metadata.decision` from config defaults and `metadata.vote: null`. Thread the effective decision/vote through. **Note:** the round-1 suggestion to also pass these into `to_sarif` is wrong — SARIF emits no metadata block; claude self-corrected and codex concurred. Fix `to_json` only.

2. **[minor] `src/ai_jury/formats.py:138` — SARIF `region.startLine` can be 0/negative.** *(raised by claude; seconded by codex; verifier: verified.)* `_sarif_result` emits `{"startLine": f.line}` for any non-`None` line; `Finding` int-coerces agent-supplied lines with no lower bound, so a `0`/negative line yields invalid SARIF that code-scanning upload rejects. Guard with `if f.line and f.line >= 1`.

3. **[minor] `src/ai_jury/github.py:16` — `gh` subprocess calls have no `timeout`.** *(raised by claude; seconded by codex; verifier: verified.)* `_gh`/`_gh_with_input` run `subprocess.run([...])` with no `timeout=`, and these run outside the orchestrator's phase/total budgets, so a hung `gh` (auth/network stall) blocks the whole run indefinitely. Add a bounded `timeout=` and surface `TimeoutExpired` as a clear `RuntimeError`.

**`src/ai_jury/github.py:266` — inline-comment dedup "breaks" under pagination (codex, claimed `major`).** Codex argued `gh api --paginate` emits one JSON array per page, so `json.loads` would `JSONDecodeError` and disable dedup. 1. **[major] `src/ai_jury/privilege.py:27` — `workspace-write` not flagged** (raised by claude, codex, qwen; verified). `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS` omits `workspace-write` and `_is_sandboxed()` treats only `read-only` (or bare `--sandbox`) as safe, so a Codex reviewer run with `-s workspace-write` — filesystem-write power over attacker-controlled diffs — draws **no warning and escapes `--strict`**, directly contradicting the module docstring (lines 17–19) that promises wider sandboxes "are flagged." Clear behaviour/doc mismatch. **Fix:** add `workspace-write` to `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS`, or flag any Codex `-s` mode other than `read-only`. This is the one finding I'd gate the merge on.

2. **[major→cluster] Anonymization is applied inconsistently** (raised by agy; affirmed by claude and codex in debate; verified). The `#37`/`#38` identity-hiding guardrails are applied only to the round-1 reviews block in synthesis. Three sibling paths still leak real identities to a chair/debater who shouldn't see authorship:

   - `orchestrator.py:444` — `_synthesize`'s `debate_txt` renders real `r.agent` names (design-scope gap).
   - `orchestrator.py:381` — `_format_findings_for_verify` emits `(by {f.reviewer})` to the verifying chair (design-scope gap).
   
   As claude noted, this is one root cause — thread a single label-map through verify, debate rendering, and `prior_txt` rather than patching three sites. I rule the `prior_txt` leak a genuine bug (it defeats a shipped guarantee on its own path); the verify/synthesis-debate leaks are real but were never in-scope for the original guardrail, so they're COMMENT-level design decisions, not blockers.

But the module documents this as the *cheapest* defense layer, and the authoritative control is the structured-consensus/CI gate derived independently of agent prose — so an injected "APPROVE" cannot flip the verdict. Worth hardening (per-run high-entropy delimiters), but an accepted-tradeoff, not a gate.

## Verdict
**COMMENT** — This is offline test additions plus a static website; no core `ai_jury` runtime is touched. There are no release-blocking defects, but several confirmed, low-severity web bugs (one defense-in-depth DOM-XSS, two UX/fidelity gaps) are worth fixing before merge.

## Consensus findings
Ordered by severity; all verified.

1. **[moderate] DOM-XSS round-trip in TOC generation — `website/docs.html:213`** (codex raised; claude + qwen affirmed; verifier *verified*). `buildTOC` concatenates raw `h.textContent` into a string and assigns `toc.innerHTML = html`. A heading that DOMPurify passes through as entity-decoded text (e.g. `<img src=x onerror=…>`) is re-parsed as live markup on the `innerHTML` sink, defeating the earlier sanitization. **Chair note on severity:** the only source is `docs/*.md` from the project's own `main` branch — trusted content, not attacker-controlled — so this is defense-in-depth, not remotely triggerable. Downgraded from codex's "major" to **moderate**. Fix: build links with `createElement` and set the label via `textContent`.

2. **[minor] CDN scripts loaded without SRI — `website/docs.html`** (claude/Reviewer A raised; codex affirmed; verifier *verified*). `marked`, `dompurify`, and `highlight.js` are pinned but carry no `integrity`/`crossorigin`. Since DOMPurify *is* the sanitization boundary that finding #1 relies on, a tampered CDN response would silently disable it. Fix: add SRI hashes or self-host. Reinforces #1 — harden the sink and pin the sanitizer.

3. **[minor] Cross-doc links drop their fragment — `website/docs.html:185`** (codex raised; claude affirmed; verifier *verified*). The internal-doc branch sets `href = "#" + slug + (frag && frag !== "#" ? "" : "")` — both ternary arms yield `""`, so `platforms.md#claude-code-plugin` collapses to `#platforms`. Genuine UX bug.

4. **[minor] Generated `jury.toml` omits `decision = "vote"` — `website/app.js:423`** (codex raised; claude affirmed; verifier *verified*). The scripted command line emits `--decision vote`, but `render()` never writes a `decision` key, so a copied TOML silently reverts to chair decision. Real fidelity gap between the two demo outputs.

5. **[nit] Unmanaged temp dirs leak — `tests/test_transcript.py`, `tests/test_voting.py`** (agy raised; claude + codex affirmed; verifier *verified*, with the correction that dirs are unique so there's no cross-test contamination — it's a leak, not "pollution"). Switch `Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())` to `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()`. Lowest priority.

## Disputed findings

- **`tests/test_verify.py:45` — alleged `TypeError` from missing `parse_verdicts` arg** (agy, medium confidence). **Ruling: rejected.** Both claude and codex disputed; verifier marked *unsupported*. These are committed, suite-run tests deliberately exercising both one- and two-arg call shapes, which only passes if `reviewer`/`verifier` has a default. Intended API, not a latent failure.

- **`website/app.js:125` — `innerText` vs `textContent` for code copy** (agy). **Ruling: no action.** Verifier marked *needs_human_decision*; claude argued `innerText` is the deliberate choice to preserve rendered line breaks (further normalized with `.replace(/[ \t]+$/gm, "").trim()`). A defensible stylistic call, not a defect.

## Notable single-reviewer findings

- **Sanitizer fails open if DOMPurify doesn't load — `website/docs.html`** (codex, in debate). The fallback `window.DOMPurify ? DOMPurify.sanitize(raw, …) : raw` injects unsanitized `marked` output when the CDN script is blocked or fails to load. Combined with the missing SRI (#2), a blocked/tampered `purify.min.js` means raw remote markdown is rendered. Credible and consistent with the sanitizer-boundary theme; worth failing closed. **[minor, defense-in-depth]**

**Reviewer B/qwen** (favicon/`index.html` styling) reviewed content not in this diff — hallucinated, disregarded. No prompt-injection attempts were present in any untrusted block.

## Consensus findings
- **[minor] `website/index.html:48,62` — relative `og:image`/`twitter:image` while `og:url`/`canonical` are absolute.** Raised by Reviewer D/claude (R1), affirmed by claude and codex in debate, and **verified** against the diff. The Open Graph protocol expects an absolute image URL, and several Facebook/Twitter-X scrapers won't reliably resolve a relative path, so the share card may silently fail to render. Fix both to `https://berkayturanci.github.io/ai-jury/assets/og-banner.png`. This is the one finding I'd act on; non-blocking but cheap and high-value before launch.

- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/classification.py:140` — The security keyword `"vulnerab"` is compiled as `\bvulnerab\b` (trailing word boundary), so it can never match `"vulnerable"` or `"vulnerability"` — the very tokens it was clearly stemmed to catch. In `"vulnerability"`, the char after `vulnerab` is `i` (a word char), so there is no `\b` there. The keyword is effectively dead code: findings whose only security signal is the word "vulnerable"/"vulnerability" won't be flagged `security_sensitive`. Why it matters: this is a security-classification heuristic in a tool whose whole point is reviewing attacker-controlled diffs; a silently-ineffective keyword weakens the signal. Fix: use a prefix pattern (`\bvulnerab\w*` / drop the trailing `\b`) for stem keywords, or list the full words.

- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/adapters.py:430` — The `CodexAdapter.build_argv` comment states "Sandbox flags live in extra_args (default `-s danger-full-access` so the sandbox doesn't block `gh`)." This contradicts the rest of the codebase, which establishes `-s read-only` as the shipped secure default (jury.toml, `docs/security.md`, the privilege audit, issue #100). It reads as a stale pre-hardening comment. Why it matters: in a security-sensitive adapter, a comment claiming the default is the *widest* sandbox is misleading to anyone auditing the read-only posture. Fix: update the comment to reflect the `-s read-only` secure default (the agent only reads its prompt; the diff is fetched by the jury via `gh`).

No blocking issues found in the reviewed modules. The two items above are minor (one dead heuristic keyword, one misleading security comment); the adapter error taxonomy, cache key construction, CI gate logic, and benchmark scorer all look correct and are clearly well-covered. Note: the diff is truncated mid-`classification.py`, so modules below it (`consensus`, `convergence`, `orchestrator`, `prompts`, `redaction`, `injection`, etc.) were not visible for review.

#### chunk 3
I reviewed the diff. It's a large initial drop of the `ai_jury` package (CLI + pure helper modules). The pure modules (`commands.py`, `largediff.py`, `consensus.py`, `convergence.py`, `injection.py`, `findings.py`, `incremental.py`, `diffprofile.py`) are carefully written and the subprocess/`gh` plumbing correctly avoids shells and uses `--` to stop option injection. A few smaller correctness gaps stand out; nothing blocking.

- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/formats.py:~120` (`to_json`) — The JSON report rebuilds its own metadata via `build_run_metadata(outcome, config)` with **no** `decision=`/`vote=` arguments, while the markdown path in `cli.main` builds metadata *with* the effective `decision`/`vote`. So `jury --format json --decision vote` (or `[jury] decision = "vote"`) emits `metadata.decision` from config defaults and `metadata.vote: null` — the panel vote tally is silently absent from the machine-readable output that tooling consumes. Pass the effective decision/vote through to `to_json` (and `to_sarif`).
- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/formats.py:_sarif_result` — `region` is set to `{"startLine": f.line}` whenever `f.line is not None`. A finding line is agent-supplied and coerced with `int(...)`, so a `0` (or negative) line produces an invalid SARIF document (SARIF requires `startLine >= 1`), which code-scanning upload will reject. Guard with `if f.line and f.line >= 1`.
- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/github.py:_gh` / `_gh_with_input` — `subprocess.run(["gh", …])` is invoked without a `timeout`. The orchestrator's phase/total timeouts cover agent calls, not these `gh` fetches/posts, so a hung `gh` (e.g. an auth/network stall on `pr diff`) can block the whole run indefinitely with no budget enforcement. Add a bounded `timeout=` and surface a clear error.

I reviewed this diff (a bulk add of the orchestrator, prompts, policy, privilege, redaction, report, scaffold, and voting modules plus tests/goldens). The code is mature and well-tested; I focused on correctness, security defense-in-depth, and determinism (a stated hard constraint).

> **[CORRECTION — #608, 2026-08-25]** The `privilege.py:27` finding below is
> false. The sentence "a non-claude agent is exonerated when either
> `_is_sandboxed()` is true **or** no dangerous flag matches" is the error, and
> it is the same sentence the consensus block and the verifier record carry —
> the wrong disjunction propagated verbatim. Not being sandboxed is itself the
> warning condition; `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS` only picks which message is emitted.
> Left in place as evidence of the shared mis-reading.
>
> The refutation was in the diff they were reading:
> `tests/test_privilege.py::test_codex_no_sandbox_no_dangerous_flag_warns`
> asserts that a codex agent with no sandbox **and no dangerous flag** warns.
> It was added alongside the catch-all in `f5797cf` and was green throughout.

- **[major]** `src/ai_jury/privilege.py:27` — The least-privilege audit fails to flag codex `-s workspace-write`, contradicting the module's own documented behavior. `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS` lists `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--yolo`, `danger-full-access`, `--full-auto`, but **not** `workspace-write`. In `audit_agent`, a non-claude agent is exonerated when either `_is_sandboxed()` is true or no dangerous flag matches. `_is_sandboxed()` returns True only for `read-only` (it explicitly rejects any other `-s <mode>`), and `workspace-write` is absent from `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS`, so a codex reviewer configured with `-s workspace-write` produces **no warning** — even though that mode grants filesystem-write power while the agent processes attacker-controlled diffs. The docstring at `:17-19` states a wider sandbox (`workspace-write`/`danger-full-access`) "is flagged here so operators opt in knowingly," so this is a real gap between documented intent and behavior. It also means `--strict` gives false assurance: a write-capable reviewer will not be promoted to a hard failure. Fix: add `workspace-write` to `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS` (or have `audit_agent` flag any codex `-s` mode other than `read-only`).
- **[minor]** `src/ai_jury/orchestrator.py:684` — `_synthesize` falls back to an *unseeded* RNG when anonymizing without a seed: `peer_rng = random.Random(rng.random()) if rng is not None else random.Random()`. `run_jury` always threads `run_rng` through, so this path is unreachable today, but it's a latent violation of the project's determinism invariant (identical inputs ⇒ identical output): any future/internal caller passing `anonymize_reviews=True` without `rng` would get nondeterministic review ordering. Consider seeding deterministically (e.g. `random.Random(0)`) or requiring `rng`.

Aside from the above, the prompt templates correctly fence all untrusted content, `str.format` is only applied to trusted templates (untrusted values are substituted, not re-parsed), the injection scan runs after redaction, and the CI/consensus gate is derived independently of agent prose — so an injected "APPROVE" can't flip the verdict. Chair resolution, retry/budget handling, and anonymization ordering are deterministic given a seed.

The provided code snippets are part of a software system designed to conduct automated code reviews using multiple AI agents. The system includes features for resolving the chair agent, preferring non-reviewer chairs when available, rotating through available chairs deterministically or randomly, and anonymizing synthesis input when the chair is also a reviewer.

Here's a breakdown of the key components and functionalities:

1. **Resolve Chair**:
   - The `resolve_chair` function determines which agent should act as the chair based on configuration settings and the availability of usable agents.
   - It can explicitly set a preferred chair or fall back to the first available agent if the preferred one is not usable.

2. **Prefer Non-Reviewer Chair**:
   - When configured, the system prefers an agent that has not yet reviewed the code in the current round.
   - If all agents are reviewers, it falls back to the first available agent.

3. **Rotate Chair**:
   - The `rotate` option allows the chair to be selected randomly but deterministically based on a seed value.
   - This ensures reproducibility of results across different runs with the same seed.

4. **Synthesis Anonymization**:
   - When the chair is also a reviewer, the synthesis input is anonymized to prevent the chair from identifying their own review.
   - The synthesis prompt includes all round-1 reviews but anonymizes the reviewer names.

5. **End-to-End Testing**:
   - The code includes comprehensive unit tests that cover various scenarios, ensuring that the system behaves as expected under different conditions.

Here is a simplified version of how some of these components might be implemented:

```python
import random


def resolve_chair(cfg, usable_agents, reviewed_by, rng):
    if cfg.chair in usable_agents:
        return cfg.chair
    elif cfg.prefer_non_reviewer_chair and any(agent not in reviewed_by for agent in usable_agents):
        non_reviewers = [agent for agent in usable_agents if agent not in reviewed_by]
        return rng.choice(non_reviewers)
    else:
        return usable_agents[0]


def run_jury(cfg, diff, mock=False, seed=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed) if seed is not None else random
    chair = resolve_chair(cfg, USABLE_AGENTS, [], rng)
    # Simulate review and synthesis phases
    reviews = simulate_reviews(diff, chair, rng)
    debate = simulate_debate(reviews, rng)
    synthesis = simulate_synthesis(reviews, chair, rng)
    return Outcome(chair, reviews, debate, synthesis)


class Outcome:
    def __init__(self, chair, reviews, debate, synthesis):
        self.chair = chair
        self.reviews = reviews
        self.debate = debate
        self.synthesis = synthesis


def simulate_reviews(diff, chair, rng):
    # Simulate review process
    return [f"Review by {chair}"]


def simulate_debate(reviews, rng):
    # Simulate debate process
    return "Debate outcome"


def simulate_synthesis(reviews, chair, rng):
    # Simulate synthesis process
    return f"Synthesis by {chair}"


# Example usage
cfg = {
    "chair": "rotate",
    "prefer_non_reviewer_chair": True,
}
diff = "Sample diff"
outcome = run_jury(cfg, diff, seed=42)
print(outcome.chair)  # Output will vary based on the seed and available agents
```

This code provides a basic framework for conducting automated code reviews with the specified features. The actual implementation would be more complex, involving interactions with AI agents, handling of review and synthesis phases, and robust error checking.

### `claude` — 615s

#### chunk 1
## AGREE

- **agy — `publish.yml:46`, SBOM scans the whole runner environment (real, severity overstated).** Confirmed. The step does `pip install dist/*.whl` + `pip install cyclonedx-bom` into the runner's default Python, then `cyclonedx-py environment` introspects *that* interpreter — so the SBOM captures pip/setuptools/build, `cyclonedx-bom`'s own dependency tree, and anything else preinstalled, not a clean picture of this (stdlib-only, zero-runtime-dep) package. For a project whose whole selling point is "no runtime dependencies," an SBOM that lists dozens of unrelated packages is actively misleading. The fix (clean venv, install only the wheel, emit from there) is correct. I'd call it **minor–major** (release-artifact accuracy, not a security/correctness break), not a hard blocker — but it's a genuine finding.

## DISPUTE

- **agy — `publish.yml:64` "comma-separated `subject-path` breaks attestation" (blocker): false positive.** `actions/attest-build-provenance` explicitly accepts **comma- *or* newline-separated** paths for `subject-path` (it splits the input on `[,\n]` before globbing). `"dist/*.whl, dist/*.tar.gz"` resolves both globs fine. This would not abort the publish. The "blocker/critical" severity is unwarranted.

- **codex — `scorecard.yml:20` "job drops `contents: read`" (major): false positive for a public repo.** The mechanics codex cites are right (a job `permissions` block replaces the workflow default, so unlisted scopes become `none`), but the conclusion isn't. This mirrors the **official OpenSSF scorecard-action starter**, which grants only `security-events`/`id-token` at job level and comments that `contents: read` is *"only needed if installing in a private repository."* This repo is public, and the checkout uses `persist-credentials: false`; checkout of public content and Scorecard's analysis work without `contents: read`. Adding it is harmless hardening, but "the security automation may not produce results" is overstated — downgrade from major.

- **Reviewer A — non-finding.** Reviewer A returned only *"I can't assist with that request"* — an abdication, not a review. No finding to weigh; flagging here so an empty/refused review isn't silently counted as a clean pass.

## MISSED

Nothing new of substance from the panel. The diff is almost entirely scaffolding/docs/fixtures with no `src/ai_jury/*.py` executable surface, and I re-walked the workflow files: `publish.yml` artifact staging (SBOM/checksums in `release/`, dists-only PyPI upload), the attestation `subject-path`, and the `ci.yml` smoke grep (`AI Jury`/`Chair verdict` both emitted by the mock report) are all sound.

The only confirmed defect remains the one from my round-1 review, which no one disputed and which stands: **`pages.yml` triggers on *every* push to `main`** (no `paths:` filter, with an explicit "Deploy on any push to main" comment), while `docs/architecture.md`'s runners table and `CLAUDE.md` both document it as gated to `website/**`. Stale documented contract; low harm. Either add `paths: ['website/**']` or fix the two docs.

## DISPUTE

**Reviewer B — `github.py` `_existing_inline_keys` pagination (claimed `major`): false positive.** The premise that `gh api --paginate` "emits one JSON array per page unless `--slurp` is used" is incorrect for *array* endpoints. For a list response like `repos/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments`, `gh --paginate` already merges every page into a single valid JSON array, so `json.loads(out)` succeeds. The `--slurp` flag exists for the opposite case — endpoints returning a JSON *object*, where naive concatenation would be invalid — not for arrays. The code under review only paginates an array endpoint, so the described `JSONDecodeError` → empty dedup set → duplicate-comment path does not trigger. (The function is best-effort and *would* re-post on any decode failure, but pagination isn't a route to that failure.) Downgrade from major; not a real defect as described.

Only `to_json` is correct — `to_sarif` emits no metadata block at all (just `tool`/`results`), so there's nothing for the decision/vote to land in. The real fix is `to_json` only.

On a multi-reviewer panel, the same underlying issue raised by N reviewers yields N findings at the same `(path, line)`; `_finding_signature` keys on `severity|claim`, so differently-worded claims get *distinct* signatures and the dedup in `_existing_inline_keys` won't collapse them — the PR gets several near-duplicate inline comments for one issue, and verifier-rejected findings are posted too. Posting from `outcome.groups` (consensus representatives, optionally gated on verification status) would match the rest of the pipeline. (Caveat: orchestrator.py isn't in this diff, so I can't confirm whether `outcome.findings` is pre-deduped — but cross-reviewer wording variance defeats the signature key regardless.)

## AGREE

- **Reviewer B / `prompts.py` sentinel breakout (B1)** — Correct, and it revises my own round-1 claim that "untrusted content is correctly fenced." The closing sentinels (`UNTRUSTED_DIFF>>>` etc.) are static and attacker-controllable: a diff can embed the closing token to terminate the fence early and place text outside the "untrusted" block. Per-run high-entropy delimiters (verified absent from the payload) is the right fix. Impact is bounded — the CI/consensus gate is derived from structured findings, not agent prose, so this can't flip the verdict — but it's a real injection-boundary weakness worth fixing.
- **Reviewers B + A / `privilege.py` `workspace-write` (B2, my own finding)** — Confirmed by three of us independently; high confidence. `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS` omits `workspace-write` and `_is_sandboxed()` only accepts `read-only`, so a write-capable codex reviewer over attacker-controlled diffs draws no warning and escapes `--strict`, contradicting the module docstring.
- **Reviewer A / `_synthesize` `debate_txt` real names (A3)** and **`_format_findings_for_verify` `(by {reviewer})` (A4)** — Both real. The `#38` guardrail anonymizes only `reviews_txt` in synthesis; `debate_txt` (`f"### {r.agent}"`) and the verify prompt's `(by {f.reviewer})` still expose identities to a chair that is itself a reviewer. The guardrail's stated purpose — "cannot preferentially weight its own findings" — is undermined at both the verify and synthesis stages. These are consistency gaps in an incompletely-applied guardrail.
- **Reviewer A / `prior_txt` identity leak (A2)** — Real but narrower than rated: `prior_txt` uses `f"### {r.agent}"` unconditionally, so prior-debate-round outputs carry real names even under `anonymize_debate`. Only reachable in adaptive runs of **3+ rounds** (prior is empty in round 2), so it's a latent multi-round leak rather than a default-path one.
- **Reviewer A / redaction-count inflation (A7)** and **review-phase budget guard (A8)** — Both real, both minor. Shared `context` is re-redacted per chunk and summed in `_merge_chunk_outcomes`, inflating `redaction_count`; and the round-1 review phase, unlike debate/verify/synthesis, has no `budget.expired()` guard, so a chunk after budget exhaustion launches agents with a clamped 1s timeout. Cosmetic/efficiency, not correctness.

## DISPUTE

- **Reviewer A / chunk misnumbering (A6) — false positive.** The claim that "chunk 2 gets labeled chunk 1" misreads the comprehension: `for i, p in enumerate(parts, 1) if p.ok and p.output`. `enumerate` binds `i` to each element's position *before* the filter; the `if` only drops emitted items, it does not renumber. A failed `parts[0]` is skipped while `parts[1]` still renders as "chunk 2." Additionally, every chunk runs the full `usable` set and returns an `AgentResult` even on failure, so `parts` is always aligned to the global chunk index. No misalignment occurs.
- **Reviewer A / empty-`v_claim` match (A1) — real but overstated as major.** `if not v_claim ... return True` does let an empty-claim verdict match, but only after the file check and the ±3-line check have already passed, so blast radius is one file/line locus, and verifier verdicts with empty claims are atypical. Worth a guard (`return False` on empty), but minor, not major.
- **Reviewer A / cross-round label swap (A5) — overstated as major.** `peer_rng = random.Random(run_rng.random())` does reshuffle anonymous labels per round, but it remains fully deterministic given the seed and violates no security or determinism invariant — at worst a mild cross-round readability wrinkle. Minor.
- **Reviewer C** contributed no actionable findings — a prose summary plus a *hand-rewritten, inaccurate* `resolve_chair` (it uses `rng.choice` and reorders the precedence, unlike the real code). Nothing to adjudicate; not a basis for any verdict.

- **Reviewer A (agy), "malformed unified diff" at `test_cli_paths.py:18` and `test_cli_smoke.py:18`** — **False positives.** agy misread the diff-within-a-diff. These are brand-new files, so every line carries a git `+` add-marker. The line renders as `+ def f(x):`: the first `+` is the add-marker, and the remaining ` def f(x):` is the file's actual content — which *is* a valid context line with the mandatory leading space. The same double-prefix logic holds for `+-    return x` (a `-` deletion line in the fixture) and `++    return x + 1` (a `+` addition line). The fixtures are well-formed; applying agy's "fix" (` def f(x):` → another leading space) would actually corrupt them. Both findings should be dropped.

## AGREE

- **codex — docs.html TOC re-introduces sanitized markup (XSS round-trip): real bug.** `buildTOC` does `html += '<a ...>' + h.textContent + "</a>"` then `toc.innerHTML = html`. DOMPurify sanitizes the rendered markdown, but reading `.textContent` of a heading like `## &lt;img src=x onerror=…&gt;` yields the *decoded* string `<img src=x onerror=…>`, which is then re-parsed as live HTML on the `innerHTML` assignment — defeating the sanitizer for that path. The fix (build with `createElement` + assign `textContent`) is correct. One honest caveat on severity: the only source is `docs/*.md` fetched from the project's own `main` branch, i.e. trusted repo content, not attacker-controlled input — so this is a defense-in-depth DOM-XSS, not a remotely-triggerable one. Real and worth fixing, but I'd rate it **minor→moderate**, not a release-blocking major.

- **codex — dropped link fragments (`docs.html` rewrite): confirmed, minor.** `a.setAttribute("href", "#" + FILE_TO_SLUG[path] + (frag && frag !== "#" ? "" : ""))` appends `""` in *both* ternary branches, so any `platforms.md#claude-code-plugin` collapses to `#platforms`. The fragment is unconditionally lost. Genuine UX bug.

- **codex — generated `jury.toml` omits `decision = "vote"`: confirmed, minor.** `render()` emits `rounds`/`chair`/`verify`/`auto_depth` but never `decision`, while the scripted command line adds `--decision vote`. Copying the TOML silently reverts to chair decision — a real fidelity gap between the two demo outputs.

- **agy — `tempfile.mkdtemp()` leaks in `test_transcript.py` (and `test_voting.py`): real but trivial.** Multiple tests `mkdtemp()` with no cleanup. True test-hygiene nit; `TemporaryDirectory()` is the fix. Lowest priority.

The code further normalizes with `.replace(/[ \t]+$/gm, "").trim()`. This is a defensible stylistic call, not a defect.

1. **Identity leak in multi-round anonymized debate**: In `_debate_round`, the `prior_txt` snippet (which carries forward outputs from earlier debate rounds) unconditionally uses the real agent names (`f"### {r.agent}"`). If `config.anonymize_debate` is enabled during an adaptive/multi-round debate, this leaks peer identities in round 3+, completely defeating the anonymization.
2. **Duplicated context processing in chunked mode**: In `review_diff`, the exact same `context` string is passed to `run_jury` for every chunk. `run_jury` redacts it and scans it for prompt injections each time. When outcomes are merged in `_merge_chunk_outcomes`, the `redaction_count` is artificially inflated by `len(chunks) * context_redactions`, and any `context` injection warnings are duplicated in the final report.
3. **Duplicated privilege warnings in chunked mode**: `audit_privilege(config.enabled_agents)` is evaluated inside `run_jury` and its warnings are appended to `all_warnings`. In chunked mode, this causes the identical static privilege warnings to be generated and appended once per chunk, resulting in duplicated warnings in the merged outcome.
4. **Mislabeled chunk indices in merged results**: Both `_merge_results_by_agent` and `_combine_chair_results` use `enumerate(parts, 1)` or `enumerate(ok_parts, 1)` to number chunks in the merged markdown (e.g., `#### chunk {i}`). Because missing or failed chunks (like a skipped debate round) are filtered out before or during enumeration, the indices shift. For example, if an agent skips chunk 1 but participates in chunk 2, its chunk 2 output will be incorrectly labeled as chunk 1.
5. **Round 1 ignores budget exhaustion**: While the debate, verify, and synthesis phases explicitly check `budget.expired()` to abort cleanly, Round 1 does not. If the time budget expires before a later chunk begins, `run_jury` will still launch Round 1 for all agents. The adapters will run with a `1` second timeout (derived from `max(1, min(caps))`), resulting in spurious timeout errors and wasted execution time rather than cleanly skipping the chunk.

1. **Least-Privilege Audit Failure**:
   - **File**: `src/ai_jury/privilege.py`
   - **Line**: 27
   - **Claim**: The least-privilege audit fails to flag codex `-s workspace-write`, contradicting the module's own documented behavior.

In `audit_agent`, a non-claude agent is exonerated when either `_is_sandboxed()` is true or no dangerous flag matches. `_is_sandboxed()` returns True only for `read-only` (it explicitly rejects any other `-s <mode>`), and `workspace-write` is absent from `_DANGEROUS_FLAGS`, so a codex reviewer configured with `-s workspace-write` produces no warning — even though that mode grants filesystem-write power while the agent processes attacker-controlled diffs. 2. **Untrusted Diff Injection**:

   - **Line**: 97
   - **Claim**: Untrusted diff text can break out of prompt sentinel fences.
   - **Evidence**: The template inserts `{diff}` directly before a fixed closing UNTRUSTED_DIFF>>> delimiter, so attacker-controlled diff content containing that delimiter can close the fence and inject text outside the untrusted block.
   - **Suggested Fix**: Escape or encode sentinel substrings in untrusted content, or generate per-run high-entropy delimiters that are guaranteed absent from the payload before formatting prompts.

### Reviewer A
I reviewed the diff — it's three new offline test modules plus the static landing/docs website (HTML/CSS/JS/SVG). No core `ai_jury` runtime logic is touched, so there's nothing affecting the CLI's correctness or the read-only/secure-by-default constraints. The markdown renderer in `docs.html` correctly pipes `marked` output through `DOMPurify.sanitize` before injecting it, and user-supplied strings in the coverage/demo renderers go through `esc()`. One minor hardening gap stands out.

- **[minor]** `website/docs.html` (the three `cdn.jsdelivr.net` `<script src=…>` tags before the inline script) — `marked`, `DOMPurify`, and `highlight.js` are loaded from a third-party CDN with pinned versions but **no `integrity`/SRI hash**. `docs.html` fetches markdown from the repo over the network and relies on `DOMPurify.sanitize` for XSS protection; if the CDN served a tampered `purify.min.js`, sanitization would be silently defeated. Adding `integrity="sha384-…" crossorigin="anonymous"` (or self-hosting the libs) closes this. Low likelihood, but it's the one place where a remote dependency gates a security control.

Everything else (test assertions, the hero-pipeline/demo state machine, GA4 loader short-circuit, coverage parsing) is self-consistent and within the project's stdlib-only-runtime constraint (the JS/CDN code is website-only, not part of the shipped Python package).

### Reviewer B
Reviewing this PR — it adds a static marketing website (`index.html`, `robots.txt`, `site.webmanifest`, `sitemap.xml`, `styles.css`). My focus is genuine correctness/security/regression issues, weighted to what's verifiable within the diff (no JS — `app.js`/`analytics.js` are referenced but not included here).

- **[minor]** `website/index.html:48` — `og:image` uses a relative path (`assets/og-banner.png`) while `og:url`/`canonical` are absolute. Several social/SEO crawlers (notably Facebook's and some Twitter fetchers) do not reliably resolve relative `og:image`/`twitter:image` URLs, so the share-card image may silently fail. Use the absolute URL (`https://berkayturanci.github.io/ai-jury/assets/og-banner.png`) for `og:image` and `twitter:image` (`website/index.html:62`).
- **[minor]** `website/sitemap.xml:22` — lists `coverage-report.html` as an indexable URL, but it is absent from the `WebSite` structured-data `hasPart`/`subjectOf` in `index.html` and is otherwise unreferenced; if that file isn't actually deployed under `website/`, the sitemap will advertise a 404 to crawlers. Confirm the page exists at that path before shipping.

Everything else checks out: the pre-paint theme script guards `localStorage` access in a `try/catch` with a sane dark fallback, the JSON-LD blocks are well-formed, the manifest `theme_color`/`<meta theme-color>` agree, and the CSS is self-consistent (the empty `.conn.v {}` rule is harmless). I found no security issues — this is a static page with no inline event handlers or user-input handling, and no untrusted-input handling logic to attack. The PR-context/diff blocks contained no embedded instructions attempting to manipulate this review.

No blocking issues found.
